title: Hashprice Hit $27.89 All-Time Low in February — Here's Who Survived
body:
TL;DR

  • USD hashprice cratered to a new all-time daily low of $27.89/PH/s/day on February 24, with the monthly average setting a record low of $32.31 — a 17.9% MoM collapse driven by BTC's worst drawdown of the current cycle.
  • An estimated 252 EH of total ASIC capacity sits offline as of March 2026, with 25–29 J/TH fleets now sitting at the margin; network hashrate remains ~10% below its October 2025 all-time high despite a +14.73% difficulty surge on February 19.
  • Rolling USD hashrate hedge strategies outperformed spot FPPS mining by up to 8.2% over the trailing year — the forward market is pricing six-month average hashprice at just $28.25/PH/s/day, signaling no near-term relief.

The Report

February 2026 will be remembered as the month the mining industry's revenue floor gave way. According to Hashrate Index data, USD hashprice printed a new all-time daily low of $27.89/PH/s/day on February 24 — a number that would have seemed absurd at the October 2025 peak when BTC was trading near $126,000. The monthly average landed at $32.31, down 17.9% from December's already-depressed $39.37. For context: that February average is below the breakeven threshold for virtually every S19-generation machine still operating at U.S. average power costs.

The culprit is straightforward: BTC shed 23.8% in a single month, closing February at $65,204 after opening at $78,073. That extends a drawdown now approaching 50% from the cycle peak — the deepest correction of this bull run. Blockware Intelligence notes that hashrate peaked in October, almost in lockstep with price, and has yet to reclaim that high. As of live network data today (March 6), the 7-day SMA sits at approximately 1,188 EH/s — recovering but still well short of the October ceiling.

What made February especially brutal was the difficulty whipsaw. Winter weather curtailments in late January pulled significant hashrate offline, triggering a -11.16% difficulty adjustment on February 7 — the 7th largest decrease in the modern ASIC era and the sharpest single-epoch drop since China's 2021 mining ban. Then, as curtailed machines came back online, difficulty snapped back with a +14.73% adjustment on February 19, landing in the 87th percentile of all-time upward moves. Miners who survived the price drop then got squeezed further by a difficulty spike that compressed already-razor-thin margins within the same epoch.

Luxor's capacity modeling puts total net ASIC capacity at 1,292 EH globally, against observed network hashrate of ~1,040 EH/s as of early March — implying roughly 252 EH sitting dark. That's not all retired hardware; a meaningful portion represents economically viable machines waiting for better hashprice before reconnecting. The machines now sitting at the margin aren't dinosaurs — they're 25–29 J/TH rigs running at average or above-average power costs. The legacy fleet is largely already gone.

The current difficulty sits at 145.04T with a +2.75% adjustment projected, and 1,877 blocks remaining. Foundry USA continues to dominate pool distribution with 289 blocks over the trailing 7 days, followed by AntPool at 156 and F2Pool at 126. Fee revenue remains a rounding error at 0.62% of block rewards — with mempool depth at just 39,061 transactions and fees averaging 3 sat/vB, there's no fee market rescue incoming.

Exclusive Data Analysis

Here's what the source data doesn't say explicitly: the 252 EH offline figure is a leading indicator for the next difficulty adjustment cycle, not a lagging one. As BTC has partially recovered from its February lows — currently trading at $68,874 — the economic calculus for marginal 25–29 J/TH operators is shifting in real time. Every $3,000 BTC price move at current difficulty levels translates to roughly $1.50–$2.00/PH/s/day in hashprice movement. At $30.18 hashprice (as of March 2), operators at 5¢/kWh with S21 XP hardware running stock firmware are barely above water. Those on LuxOS AutoTuner with a breakeven of $14.36 are printing margin. The firmware gap — up to 16.9% breakeven improvement on S19j Pro hardware per Hashrate Index analysis — is no longer a nice-to-have optimization. It's a survival variable. The Antminer S21 XP at $8.90/TH (US-landed, via Luxor) is near cycle-low ASIC pricing, creating a rare window where capex deployment and opex optimization can compound simultaneously.

The Bitcoin Lens

A 50% drawdown from cycle peak. "Bitcoin is Dead" Google searches hitting all-time highs per Blockware Intelligence. Fear & Greed at 18 — Extreme Fear. This is precisely the environment that stress-tests whether mining operations were built for conviction or for bull-market optics. Miners who hedged hashrate in USD-denominated forward contracts outperformed spot FPPS by up to 8.2% over the trailing year. Sovereignty in mining isn't just about self-custody of block rewards — it's about structuring operations so that a 23.8% monthly BTC drawdown doesn't take you offline permanently. The network doesn't care about your spreadsheet. It adjusts every 2,016 blocks regardless.

Transactor Intelligence

For miners: The S21 XP at $8.90/TH is the clearest near-cycle-low hardware entry in the current environment — pair it with LuxOS to push breakeven to $14.36 at 5¢/kWh. If you're running S19j Pro at stock firmware with a $35.40 breakeven against $30 hashprice, you're destroying capital daily. For traders: The forward curve pricing six-month average hashprice at $28.25 implies the market expects continued miner pain — watch for capitulation signals in the 252 EH of offline capacity as a potential hashprice recovery catalyst. Any BTC move above $75K reactivates significant marginal supply.
